answer: The default synonymy threshold is τ = 0.8, tuned on 100 MuSiQue training examples [2405.14831#s11.p1]. HippoRAG 2 also uses a synonym threshold of 0.8 [2502.14802#s39.p3].
The survey ultimately selected 218 key articles, covering publications from 2023 Q1 to 2025 Q4 [2602.06052#s6.p1].

HippoRAG treats the knowledge graph as a hippocampal index: an LLM (the 'neocortex') extracts schemaless KG triples via OpenIE, and the open KG serves as the index of interconnected pointers with associations, enabling pattern separation at encoding and pattern completion at retrieval [2405.14831#s5.p1][2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s4.p1]. Because the index is a graph, multi-hop reasoning can happen in a single retrieval step [2405.14831#s2.p5]. On its graph HippoRAG runs Personalized PageRank: query entities are linked to KG nodes, PPR is seeded with a distribution uniform on those query nodes, and the resulting node distribution is multiplied by the passage-node count matrix to score passages [2405.14831#s6.p2][2405.14831#s6.p4]; node specificity scales query-node probabilities before PPR, and the damping factor is 0.5 [2405.14831#s6.p5][2405.14831#s11.p1]. The agent-memory survey, by contrast, does not single out knowledge graphs as the memory substrate; it organizes memory by substrate (external vector/text/structural/hierarchical stores vs. internal weights, latent state, KV cache), cognitive mechanism (sensory, working, episodic, semantic, procedural), and subject, and notes that no single substrate dominates so effective designs are hybrid [2602.06052#s2.p2][2602.06052#s17.p6]. The ingested corpus does not contain a statement from that survey specifically conceptualizing knowledge graphs' role in memory systems.

On 2WikiMultiHopQA, HippoRAG (ColBERTv2) reaches R@5 of 89.1 versus 65.6 for ColBERTv2 on average, and the paper reports gains of about 20 points on 2Wiki [2405.14831#s12.p3][2405.14831#s12.p6]. The survey/HippoRAG 2 paper identifies as a limitation that prior structure-augmented RAG methods (RAPTOR, GraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG) improve sense-making or associativity but degrade on basic factual memory, falling below the strongest embedding-based RAG on all three benchmark types; each method type decays most outside its own setup, e.g., HippoRAG drops most on discourse understanding for lack of query-based contextualization [2502.14802#s2.p6].

In SSGM's Principle 4 (Reversible Reconciliation), the append-only structure serving as the operational source of truth is the Immutable Episodic Log, paired with a Mutable Active Graph for fast semantic reasoning [2603.11768#s22.p1]. It is also denoted K_ledger, the operational raw trace used for correction [2603.11768#s23.p10].
The ingested corpus does not contain this information.

CUPMem handles older memories at write time via state adjudication rather than query-time reconciliation. An LLM adjudicator assigns each candidate old state one of KEEP, STALE, REPLACE, or UNKNOWN [2605.06527#s15.p1]. Stale states are archived rather than deleted, and unsafe slots without a settled replacement are marked UNKNOWN_CURRENT [2605.06527#s63.p10]. A topology-triggered search then expands invalidation to structurally affected state regions, so propagated conflicts are retired before query time [2605.06527#s15.p1]. At readout, only authorized state is consumed: active items ground answers, stale items serve as historical context, and unresolved slots block unsafe old defaults [2605.06527#s15.p1]. This raises overall accuracy from 8.7% to 68.0% under the same GPT-4o-mini backbone [2605.06527#s15.p1].

The two papers disagree on the headline verdict. The preregistered agent-browsed comparison (24 papers, 13 questions) does not crown a winner: the wiki's synthesis advantage fell below the registered +2.0 threshold (+1.625 judge-averaged on structural_integrity), point-source groundedness parity was fragile (+0.667 judge-averaged, P(mu≥0)=0.660), and corrected claim-level citation support actually favored RAG (53.8% vs 41.5% supported) [2605.18490#s26.p2][2605.18490#s27.p3][2605.18490#s37.p6]. The classroom comparison (59 questions) reports the opposite: the compiled wiki leads vector RAG overall (9.95 vs 9.05 of 10; grounded 98% vs 81%) and even on topic-page questions (9.96 vs 9.33), with the advantage roughly tripling on cross-page questions [2609.25303#s16.p2][2609.25303#s16.p5][2609.25303#s16.p6].

The key factor they identify is the wiki arm's serving/context-selection strategy. In the classroom study the wiki arm has no context-selection step that can fail, so the authors read the gap as the difference between real retrieval and perfect context selection, and treat their result as directional rather than general [2609.25303#s24.p3]. The agent-browsed comparison instead has a tool-using agent pay for its own traversal (up to 30 turns), which reverses the cost verdict relative to retrieved-pages serving [2605.18490#s8.p1]. More broadly, the concept page attributes the disagreement to 'wiki' and 'RAG' naming families of systems rather than operating points, with verdicts depending on serving strategy, baseline, scoring, and judge [2605.18490#s8.p1].

HippoRAG 2 exposes knowledge as a graph index: an LLM extracts schemaless OpenIE triples whose subjects/objects are phrase nodes and edges are relation edges, plus synonym edges between similar phrases and passage nodes linked by "contains" context edges, forming an open KG with sparse conceptual and dense contextual coding [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. Retrieval seeds this graph (query-to-triple matching, LLM triple filtering) and ranks passages with Personalized PageRank [2502.14802#s9.p1][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. LLM-Wiki instead exposes knowledge as a persistent, human-readable wiki: directory indices, structured Markdown pages, and source archives, where each page carries metadata, aliases, tags, facts, source references, and bidirectional wikilinks [2605.25480#s9.p1]. Retrieval is agent-planned compositional traversal via wiki_search/wiki_read tools rather than a single graph-ranking step [2605.25480#s11.p2][2605.25480#s12.p2]. So the structural artifact differs: HippoRAG 2 uses an OpenIE knowledge graph with phrase/passage nodes and PPR; LLM-Wiki uses a linked Markdown wiki with directory indices and bidirectional wikilinks (plus an Error Book for self-correction) [2605.25480#s8.p1][2605.25480#s9.p1].

LLM-Wiki achieves the higher MuSiQue F1: 0.739, versus 0.659 for LightRAG (the strongest baseline cited) [2605.25480#s24.p2]. The LLM-Wiki paper reports its MuSiQue gain over LightRAG as 8.1 F1 points [2605.25480#s24.p3]. Note that the HippoRAG 2 paper itself reports 48.6 F1 on MuSiQue [2502.14802#s14.p8], but the LLM-Wiki paper's own baseline table does not give a HippoRAG 2 MuSiQue F1, so a direct LLM-Wiki-vs-HippoRAG 2 MuSiQue margin is not stated in the corpus.

The corpus does not report an absolute 2WikiMultiHopQA F1 for HippoRAG 2. It only states that HippoRAG 2 beats NV-Embed-v2 by 9.5% F1 on 2Wiki [2502.14802#s17.p2], and the per-dataset F1 list (NQ 63.3, MuSiQue 48.6, HotpotQA 75.5, LV-Eval 12.9, NarrativeQA 25.9) omits 2WikiMultiHopQA [2502.14802#s14.p8].
The classification head achieves AUROC 0.728 (F1 0.212) on the held-out finance test set for predicting abnormal stock volatility [2606.09877#s64.p2][2606.09877#s64.p3].

WiCER instantiates CEGAR reactively: the document collection is the concrete system, the wiki the abstraction, a score-1 diagnostic probe is the counterexample, and pinning the refinement—so refinement is driven by observed QA failures [2605.07068#s37.p1][2605.07068#s36.p1]. Streaming Knowledge Compilation (Online WiCER) replaces this probe-driven reactive pinning with proactive pinning driven by a predicted materiality signal φ̂_t, which scores a document's informational importance for an entity and serves as a query-relevance surrogate, so facts are pinned before any query exposes a gap [2606.09877#s2.p3][2606.09877#s2.p2]. It also adds decay-weighted eviction and periodic full recompilation every T_r steps, with O(√(T log K)) regret plus a prediction-error term [2606.09877#s31.p2][2606.09877#s43.p3]. The key conceptual shift is 'predictive CEGAR': the counterexample is no longer an observed QA failure but a predicted high-materiality news item, moving refinement from diagnosis to prediction [2606.09877#s42.p1][2606.09877#s42.p4].

The paper identifies a pervasive LLM-as-judge confound on post-training facts: when gold answers post-date the judge backbone's training cutoff, the judge rewards fluent, confident parametric answers over factual grounding, so absolute QA scores can invert (e.g., No Wiki scoring highest at 3.90 vs. Oracle 3.67) [2606.09877#s78.p3][2606.09877#s77.p3]. Instead of absolute QA scores, it proposes regret analysis on matched pairs as the reliable metric for compiled knowledge systems [2606.09877#s1.p1][2606.09877#s78.p4].

WiCER recovers 80% of the quality lost by blind compilation on average (mean 3.24 vs. 3.47 full-context raw over the 15 topics with baselines) [2605.07068#s39.p2]. Online WiCER reaches a finance cumulative regret of −20.0 (−0.12/step) over 173 matched pairs [2606.09877#s78.p5][2606.09877#s78.p7].
82 of the 356 repositories (23.0%, 95% CI 18.8–27.2%) contained at least one stale code element reference [2606.09090#s9.p4].

HippoRAG 2 does not use downstream feedback to improve its structured knowledge base. Its graph is built offline from LLM-extracted OpenIE triples, with synonym edges and passage nodes added [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2], and retrieval uses query-to-triple matching, an LLM triple filter, and Personalized PageRank [2502.14802#s9.p1][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. The graph is a fixed index with no described mechanism for revision based on downstream retrieval or QA performance.

WikiLoop explicitly couples construction to downstream use, motivated by the fact that construction normally receives no signal from downstream use [2607.26604#s1.p1]. Its Builder reward is the marginal change in navigation utility: each patch is applied to an isolated copy and a frozen Navigator is run on both states, giving ΔU_affected and ΔU_guard [2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p12]. The reward subtracts a one-sided guard penalty for regressions on unrelated queries plus edit-cost and structure penalties [2607.26604#s7.p14]; this guarded marginal-utility credit cuts guard regression from 0.046 to 0.016 while affected ΔAC stays near 12 [2607.26604#s12.p12].

In short, HippoRAG 2's structured graph is built once and not refined by downstream feedback, whereas WikiLoop makes downstream navigation utility the direct training signal for each knowledge-base edit [2607.26604#s7.p2][2607.26604#s7.p14].
WikiLoop achieves higher All AC on AuthTrace: 62.6 versus LLM-Wiki, base, a margin of 6.3 points [2607.26604#s11.p4].
ChronoMem achieves Recall@1 of 20.5% for semantic version selection on LoCoMo (versus 12.0% for the Hybrid RRF baseline) [2607.27773#s32.p4].

The page reports HippoRAG 2's retrieval recall@5 averages 78.2 versus 73.4 for NV-Embed-v2, with a gain of 5.0 on MuSiQue [2502.14802#s14.p10][2502.14802#s17.p3]. The exact MuSiQue Recall@5 value itself is not stated numerically—only the +5.0 improvement over NV-Embed-v2 is given.

Last-write-wins achieves the same substring exact match as TEPA-Rev: both reach 0.890 substring EM on MemoryAgentBench SH-6k (versus 0.630 for TEPA-NoRev and 0.583 for append-only) [2608.07429#s31.p3].
The two-sided exact McNemar p-value is p = 2.56×10⁻⁶ (3 vs 29 errors over 300 paired queries) [2610.05732#s24.p4].

ReFind retrieves via an agent-controlled, iterative ReAct loop over a lexical BM25 index at turn granularity: the LLM chooses keywords and parameters across up to 4 rounds, with four chat-native controls (RRF session fusion, ±2-turn context expansion, temporal filtering, and seen-session deduplication) [2608.12888#s10.p1][2608.12888#s22.p1][2608.12888#s13.p5][2608.12888#s15.p1][2608.12888#s16.p1][2608.12888#s17.p1]. Raw-RAG instead uses a single-shot, non-agentic dense pipeline: 256-token windows with 32-token overlap are embedded in a flat index, the question retrieves the 128 nearest windows by cosine similarity, a cross-encoder reranks them, and the top 15 go to the reader [2610.30755#s6.p2][2610.30755#s6.p3]. So the key difference is agent-controlled multi-round lexical search with chat-native controls versus one-shot dense retrieval plus reranking over fixed chunks [2608.12888#s18.p1][2610.30755#s6.p3].

Agent Zero Memory treats knowledge updates as versioned, provenance-bearing assertions rather than overwrites: it records each assertion with its origin, evidence, and calibrated belief, and its citation-lock requires answers to cite only items actually opened, structurally excluding fabrication [2608.29606#s6.p2][2608.29606#s6.p3][2608.29606#s6.p4]. It criticizes systems that "overwrite silently or accrete contradictions" and emphasizes epistemic loss when updates overwrite rather than version [2608.29606#s1.p2][2608.29606#s3.p7]. Its design principle is provenance with calibrated belief under the citation lock, plus layering of raw sources, curated facts, and inferred experience [2608.29606#s6.p5].

Raw-RAG takes the opposite stance: it indexes raw history without LLM-based extraction, summarization, graph construction, or mutation, leaving evidence interpretation and state reconstruction to the reader [2610.30755#s6.p1][2610.30755#s6.p2]. It does not model supersession at all—no facts are extracted or updated—and adding atomic-fact extraction, summary augmentation, or graph expansion actually reduces performance (by 19.62, 5.81, and 5.78 points) [2610.30755#s12.p1]. Its design principle is that naive dense-retrieval-plus-reranking over unprocessed history is a strong baseline, achieving the highest evidence coverage (45.29% on MemoryAgentBench, 76.35% on MEME) and outperforming agentic memory systems in six of seven benchmark–model settings [2610.30755#s1.p1][2610.30755#s15.p7].

WorldDB is the engine-layer comparator that excludes all three write-time anomalies (N1, N2, N3) only by keeping the judge off the write path; TOKI alone excludes all three while keeping the judge on it [2606.06240#s17.p4].

On the four evolving-knowledge benchmarks (code_mutation, config_migration, dependency_bump, api_evolution), MemStrata (temporal_v6) reaches 1.00, 1.00, 1.00, and 0.95 accuracy, versus standard RAG's 0.43, 0.25, 0.20, and 0.40 [2606.26511#s13.p2]. So MemStrata spans 0.95–1.00 while RAG spans 0.20–0.43.

HippoRAG associates information across passages at index/retrieval time: an LLM extracts schemaless OpenIE triples from each passage into a knowledge graph, synonymy edges link similar noun phrases, and retrieval runs Personalized PageRank over this graph to score passages, so knowledge is integrated across passage boundaries rather than each passage being encoded in isolation [2405.14831#s2.p3][2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s6.p4]. TOKI instead treats contradictions as write-time concurrency control: a bitemporal fact (subject-predicate-object with valid-time, system-time, provenance, confidence) contradicts another when they share subject/predicate, differ in object, and their valid-time periods overlap; typed operators (last-writer-wins, evidence-weighted merge, await-confirmation, per-rule policy) pick a winner, invalidate the loser in system time, and emit an audit tuple, with each operator carrying an isolation precondition and admitted anomalies [2606.06240#s6.p1][2606.06240#s10.p1][2606.06240#s2.p1]. So HippoRAG's mechanism is graph-based associative indexing and PPR propagation across passages, whereas TOKI's is a bitemporal operator algebra with isolation levels, audit rows, and keyed judge logs for resolving conflicting writes [2606.06240#s1.p1][2606.06240#s15.p2].

Both studies find that LLM summarization at write time does not pay off relative to cheaper alternatives, though for different reasons.

3x3 study (2603.02473): Write strategy matters little — accuracy spans only 3–8 points across write strategies versus 20 points across retrieval methods [2603.02473#s1.p1]. The zero-LLM-call Basic RAG (raw chunks) matches or beats the costlier MemGPT-style Summarized Episodes and Mem0-style Extracted Facts under cosine (77.9%) and hybrid (81.1%), with the sole exception of BM25, where Summarized Episodes (62.7%) edges out Basic RAG (59.2%) [2603.02473#s8.p1]. The authors argue lossy compression discards details the backbone can otherwise use, and improving retrieval yields larger gains than write-time sophistication [2603.02473#s8.p1].

MERIT (2609.05441): LLM summarization behaves like update-on-write and does help on updated facts — C3 (LLM summary) reaches 1.00/0.70/1.00 on hard tasks, far above retrieval's 0.35–0.70, and C3−C2 is +0.44/+0.38/+0.28 across models (all p≤0.0002) [2609.05441#s22.p4][2609.05441#s29.p5]. But it is not the most cost-effective: the structured fact store C4 has the best CAMU in two of three domains, and full replay is never economical [2609.05441#s26.p1]. So summarization pays off only for fact-update robustness, not as the best write strategy overall.

The two papers treat the link differently. The Missing Knowledge Layer paper ties contradiction resolution to persistence semantics by making supersession the Knowledge layer's persistence mechanism: facts are "superseded, not forgotten," with old claims preserved and linked to successors with provenance [2604.11364#s8.p1], and Knowledge's persistence is "Indefinite; supersession" with append-only + provenance updates [2604.11364#s7.p3]. It argues conflating layers causes a category error—applying cognitive decay to factual claims or identical update mechanics to facts and experiences [2604.11364#s1.p1]—and notes BEAM shows all systems scoring worst on contradiction resolution (<0.05) at 10M tokens, an architectural rather than retrieval problem [2604.11364#s13.p6]. Its pilot shows typed routing (separating Knowledge from Memory) improves contradiction resolution 0.500 vs 0.394 [2604.11364#s20.p9].

TOKI instead frames contradiction resolution as write-time concurrency control: the four production heuristics (last-writer-wins, evidence-weighted merge, await-confirmation, per-rule policy) are one family of bitemporal operators, each with an undeclared isolation precondition and admitted write-time anomalies [2606.06240#s1.p1][2606.06240#s2.p1]. Persistence semantics enter via the bitemporal fact (valid-time and system-time periods, provenance, confidence) [2606.06240#s6.p1] and the dual-row schema where the loser is invalidated in system time and an audit row preserves the overwritten fact [2606.06240#s10.p1][2606.06240#s9.p1]; audit erasure (N3) is the anomaly of losing that record [2606.06240#s11.p1]. So the Missing Knowledge Layer paper makes supersession-with-provenance the defining persistence semantics of the Knowledge layer, while TOKI specifies contradiction resolution as an isolation-indexed write-time contract whose persistence requirement is a bitemporal audit trail of invalidations.

In the ConstraintRot benchmark, control violation is 0% for every model, and a single compaction step raises pooled violation to 30% across the seven models (up to 59% on DeepSeek-V4 and Kimi-K2.5) [2606.22528#s18.p1][2606.22528#s18.p3].

On deepseek-v3 Large, timestamp re-ranking scores 20.3% conflict-resolution accuracy versus 56.8% for standard RAG — i.e., timestamp re-ranking is 36.5 points worse than standard RAG [2609.16073#s14.p3]. (For context, GC-Mem reaches 97.3% in the same cell [2609.16073#s14.p3].) Timestamp heuristics blindly penalize all historical chunks, discarding valid non-contradicted facts along with stale ones [2609.16073#s14.p1].

HippoRAG organizes long-term memory as an LLM-extracted knowledge graph used as a hippocampal index: an instruction-tuned LLM extracts schemaless KG triples from passages via OpenIE, synonymy edges are added by embedding similarity, and retrieval runs Personalized PageRank over the graph to score passages [2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s6.p1][2405.14831#s6.p4]. It is a graph-index over passages, not a wiki.

TrajWiki instead compiles dialogue memory into a persistent wiki layer: immutable episodic snapshots are grouped into append-only trajectories, and these are organized into wiki pages of four types (index, entity, topic, inventory) [2608.00967#s7.p1][2608.00967#s7.p2][2608.00967#s8.p3][2608.00967#s8.p5]. Retrieval is hierarchical rather than graph-based: a query is routed to top wiki pages, whose links induce candidate trajectories, which are then expanded into provenance-linked snapshots and source messages [2608.00967#s9.p2][2608.00967#s9.p5][2608.00967#s9.p8].

So the key contrast: HippoRAG uses a knowledge graph plus PPR for single-step multi-hop retrieval over a static corpus [2405.14831#s1.p1], while TrajWiki uses a wiki of pages linking to evolving memory trajectories, preserving provenance and source grounding for long-horizon dialogue [2608.00967#s1.p1][2608.00967#s2.p2].

Yes, they agree. The survey states that no single substrate dominates — internal memory is low-latency but costly to update and prone to forgetting, external memory scales but adds retrieval latency and embedding/ranking sensitivity — so effective designs are hybrid [2602.06052#s17.p4][2602.06052#s17.p5][2602.06052#s17.p6]. The Harness the Memory evaluation likewise concludes "No substrate dominates": leadership reverses by benchmark and model band (e.g., M5 leads LoCoMo/LME-S, M3 leads TTL, M7 peaks on ALFWorld, M2 overtakes M5 on BCB-Hard at ~1/6 latency) [2608.15008#s11.p1][2608.15008#s12.p1][2608.15008#s12.p2], and retrieval breadth also reverses across regimes [2608.15008#s15.p1]. Both therefore support regime-dependent, portfolio/hybrid substrate selection rather than one dominant substrate.

They differ in whether conflicting/stale information is actively removed. GC-Mem treats memory as mutable state and explicitly resolves conflicts: it detects contradictions among retrieved candidates with an NLI oracle and applies a temporal-dominance operator that excises older contradictory chunks, so only the newest valid state survives [2609.16073#s9.p4][2609.16073#s9.p5]. This targets "semantic shadowing," where stale and updated states are semantically equivalent and dense retrieval returns the majority of stale chunks [2609.16073#s2.p2]. Its effectiveness is bounded by conflict-detector recall, not precision [2609.16073#s16.p3][2609.16073#s20.p1]. HippoRAG 2, by contrast, is a non-parametric continual-learning retrieval framework: it builds an offline OpenIE knowledge graph with passage and synonym edges and retrieves via query-to-triple matching, LLM triple filtering, and Personalized PageRank [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s9.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. It handles new information by indexing it into the graph and filtering retrieved triples for relevance [2502.14802#s10.p1]; the pages describe no explicit mechanism for detecting or pruning contradictory/stale memories.

The paper is A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents (arXiv 2502.12110). It links an agent's notes to each other following the Zettelkasten method — atomic notes, flexible linking, and continuous evolution of the knowledge network [2502.12110#s6.p1]. Zettelkasten is the note-taking system of German sociologist Niklas Luhmann. In A-Mem, each note stores LLM-generated keywords, tags, and context plus an embedding and a set of linked memories [2502.12110#s7.p2][2502.12110#s7.p3]; for a new note, cosine similarity selects top-k candidates and the LLM decides which links to create [2502.12110#s8.p2][2502.12110#s8.p6].

LightMem: Lightweight and Efficient Memory-Augmented Generation (arXiv 2510.18866). It is inspired by the Atkinson–Shiffrin model of human memory and organizes memory into three stages—sensory memory, short-term memory (STM), and long-term memory (LTM)—to cut token consumption and API calls [2510.18866#s1.p1][2510.18866#s6.p1]. Its sleep-time LTM update decouples memory updates from inference [2510.18866#s9.p1], and it reduces cost by up to 38× tokens and 30× API calls [2510.18866#s13.p2].

HaluMem is the benchmark: it is the first operation-level hallucination evaluation benchmark for memory systems, scoring memory extraction, memory updating, and memory question answering separately with stage-specific gold standards, so it can detect fabricated facts at store (extraction), update, and answer stages [2511.03506#s1.p1][2511.03506#s6.p8]. Its metrics include False Memory Resistance for extraction (fraction of distractors ignored) and hallucination rates for updating and QA [2511.03506#s12.p2][2511.03506#s14.p6][2511.03506#s15.p5].

LongMemEval tests five long-term memory abilities: (1) information extraction — recalling specific details from extensive histories, including those stated by the assistant; (2) multi-session reasoning — synthesizing/aggregating and comparing information across sessions; (3) knowledge updates — recognizing changes in user information over time; (4) temporal reasoning — using explicit time mentions and timestamp metadata; and (5) abstention — answering "I don't know" for unmentioned information [2410.10813#s8.p2]. These are operationalized by seven question types plus 30 false-premise abstention questions [2410.10813#s8.p3].
RAPTOR + GPT-4 reaches 82.6% accuracy on QuALITY overall and 76.2% on the HARD subset [2401.18059#s16.p2].

Hindsight reports 91.4% on LongMemEval (with Gemini-3), the best of its reported configurations; with OSS-120B it reaches 89.0% and with OSS-20B 83.6% on the LongMemEval S setting [2512.12818#s62.p2]. A later comparison (Agent Zero Memory) also cites Hindsight at 91.40% on LongMemEval [2608.29606#s17.p3].

Against the naive retrieval baseline (NaiveRAG) on the Agriculture dataset, LightRAG's overall win rate is 67.6% [2410.05779#s11.p3]. (An independent audit reports this 66.70% figure falls to 39.06% under a bias-controlled protocol [2506.06331#s20.p2].)

RAPTOR (Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval) builds a tree by recursively embedding, clustering, and summarizing chunks of text, so retrieval can draw on different levels of abstraction [2401.18059#s1.p1][2401.18059#s8.p3]. Clustered nodes are siblings and a parent node holds the summary of that cluster [2401.18059#s2.p2], and querying across levels lets information be retrieved at the granularity the question needs [2401.18059#s11.p7].

The paper is "From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization" (GraphRAG). It targets global questions aimed at an entire corpus, a query-focused summarization task rather than explicit retrieval [2404.16130#s1.p1][2404.16130#s2.p1]. Its LLM-built graph index derives an entity knowledge graph and then pregenerates community summaries for groups of closely related entities; each community summary yields a partial response that is summarized into a final answer [2404.16130#s1.p1]. Communities come from hierarchical Leiden detection, enabling divide-and-conquer summarization [2404.16130#s13.p1][2404.16130#s13.p2].

"Don't Do RAG: When Cache-Augmented Generation is All You Need for Knowledge Tasks" (Huang et al., arXiv 2412.15605) proposes cache-augmented generation: it preloads all relevant documents into a long-context LLM and precomputes the key-value (KV) cache encapsulating the model's inference state, then answers queries with no retrieval step [2412.15605#s2.p3][2412.15605#s3.p2]. The cost is paid once regardless of query count, eliminating retrieval latency and retrieval errors [2412.15605#s3.p2].

MemoryAgentBench tests four competencies: Accurate Retrieval (AR), Test-Time Learning (TTL), Long-Range Understanding (LRU), and Selective Forgetting (SF) [2507.05257#s2.p2]. AR is extracting the correct snippet for a query (one-hop or multi-hop); TTL is acquiring new behaviors/skills during deployment without additional training; LRU is integrating information across extended contexts (≥100k tokens) for global understanding; SF is revising, overwriting, or removing stored information when faced with contradictory evidence [2507.05257#s2.p2].
